01.event: After a reservoir at Yavne was measured and found short of the ritual-bath minimum, Tarfon and Akiva disagreed over whether past immersions in it counted, and argued it out with parables and analogies.
01.turn: Akiva offered a second line of reasoning (the bath's disqualification comes from itself, not from others) that answered Tarfon's analogy.
01.outcome: Tarfon accepted Akiva's reasoning and said that whoever parts from him parts from life.
01.summary: A reservoir in Yavne, presumed to hold the required amount, was measured and found deficient. Rabbi Tarfon declared the earlier immersions pure and Rabbi Akiva declared them impure, and each argued his case with a parable about a disqualified priest. Akiva's second argument won Tarfon over, and Tarfon told him that anyone who separates from him separates from life.

02.actor: A man who rented out a millstone and the man who rented it
02.event: A millstone owner who had been paid by the renter's grinding grew rich, bought his own millstone and donkey, and demanded money rent from the renter.
02.turn: The owner no longer needed the grinding service and demanded cash; the renter insisted he would only grind as agreed.
02.outcome: The passage leaves the dispute unresolved; no ruling is given in the passage itself.
02.summary: A man rented out a millstone in exchange for grinding done for him. He later grew rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and no longer needed the grinding, so he told the renter to pay money instead. The renter replied that he would grind as agreed but had not agreed to pay cash.
02.missing: How the dispute was decided; the context only discusses it legally.

03.event: Rabbi Eliezer missed the study hall, met Rabbi Asi, asked what was said there, and heard that Rabbi Yohanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei.
03.turn: Eliezer inferred from the ruling that only a single authority disagreed with Rabbi Yosei.
03.outcome: Rabbi Asi confirmed with a baraita (in the context), but the anecdote serves a legal argument and has no real ending.
03.summary: Rabbi Eliezer did not attend the study hall one day, so he asked Rabbi Asi, whom he met standing, what had been said. Asi reported Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Eliezer inferred that only one person must have disagreed, and Asi said yes, citing a baraita.
03.missing: The anecdote is only a frame for a legal question; there is no real story arc.

04.actor: A woman who seized a silver cup, and Rava
04.event: A widow seized a silver cup against her marriage contract and also demanded sustenance, and brought the matter to Rava.
04.turn: Rava dismissed the worry about Rabbi Shimon's view that part of a sum does not count as the whole.
04.outcome: Rava ordered the orphan heirs to give her sustenance.
04.summary: A woman took a silver cup as partial payment of her marriage contract and also asked for sustenance from the heirs. She went to Rava, who told the orphans to give her sustenance, since nobody follows Rabbi Shimon's view that part of the money is not treated like all of it.

05.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could climb onto and off her bed using him as a step, and boasted of this in the study hall.
05.turn: The sages told him he had not reached even half of true honor, because he had not borne her throwing a purse into the sea in front of him without shaming her.
05.outcome: He was deflated by the rebuke; no further outcome is stated.
05.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend over so his mother could step on him to climb into and out of bed. He praised himself for this in the study hall, and the sages replied that he had not yet reached half of the honor due, since he had never faced her throwing his purse into the sea without embarrassing her.

06.actor: Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Hanina and a man who kissed Yonatan's foot
06.event: A man bent and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot as Yonatan and Hanina stood together, and Hanina asked why.
06.turn: Yonatan explained the man had written his property over to his sons and Yonatan had forced the sons to feed him.
06.outcome: The Gemara reads the story as showing that the law does not follow Rabbi Ile'a, because forcing the sons implies they were not obligated.
06.summary: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing together when a man came and kissed Yonatan's foot. Hanina asked what this was, and Yonatan said the man had given his property to his sons and Yonatan had made them feed him. The Gemara uses this to prove the law is not as Rabbi Ile'a held.

07.missing: It describes Rav Huna's habitual practice of asking for a substitute worker before judging, not a single event with a turn and an ending.

08.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava, and Rav Neḥemya
08.event: A widow came before Rav Neḥemya and asked for sustenance and then wine, and he granted both.
08.turn: He justified granting wine by the local custom of Mehoza residents drinking wine.
08.outcome: She was awarded sustenance and wine.
08.summary: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Neḥemya and asked for sustenance, which he granted. She then asked for wine, and he granted that too, saying he knew the people of Mehoza drink wine.
08.missing: It is a very short case report with only a slight turn.

09.actor: Rav Yosef and his student Abaye
09.event: Rav Yosef, who had forgotten his learning after illness, said he had never heard a halakha about roofs, and Abaye reminded him that he had taught it.
09.turn: Abaye recounted what Yosef had said, which brought it back to Yosef's memory.
09.outcome: Rav Yosef recalled it and restated his teaching, correcting the version Abaye gave, and answered Abaye's follow-up challenge.
09.summary: Rav Yosef, who had forgotten some of his learning, said he had never heard a certain ruling on roofs. His student Abaye said that Yosef himself had taught it, and recited it. Yosef then remembered and clarified what he had actually said, and answered Abaye's objection about residents.
09.missing: Most of the passage is the legal content of the remembered teaching.

10.missing: It is a question put to Rabbi Eliezer and his quip in reply; nothing happens beyond a question and answer.

11.event: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called first his younger son Shimon and then his older son Gamliel and gave each his instructions.
11.turn: He passed on wisdom to one son and the office of Nasi, with advice to rule firmly, to the other.
11.outcome: Both sons received their transmission; the death itself is not within the text shown.
11.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi neared death he asked for his younger son, Rabbi Shimon, and passed on the orders of wisdom to him. He then asked for his older son, Rabban Gamliel, gave him the procedures of the office of Nasi, and told him to lead firmly and cast fear on the students.
11.missing: The beginning of the death narrative and its end are not in the passage.

12.missing: It is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel; the case of Pishon the camel driver is only cited as a precedent, with no event told.

13.actor: Rav Yosef and two rival claimants to a field
13.event: Two deeds on the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and the other just Nisan, and he awarded the field to the one with the specific date.
13.turn: The losing claimant objected, and Rav Yosef pointed out his deed could be read as dated the twenty-ninth of Nisan.
13.outcome: The loser asked for a document authorizing repossession, and the Gemara settles on both writing authorizations for each other.
13.summary: Two buyers of the same field came to Rav Yosef, one with a deed dated the fifth of Nisan and one dated only Nisan. Rav Yosef gave the field to the specific date, and told the other his deed might be from the twenty-ninth. The loser asked for authorization to repossess later-sold property, Rav Yosef noted a flaw in that, and the Gemara proposed that they authorize each other.

14.missing: It only reports how many blessings two sages recited at weddings; nothing turns or ends.

15.missing: It is a chain of reported rulings by visiting sages on a legal question, with no story told.

16.event: A person came before Rav Yosef, who told the heirs to give a daughter her sustenance from dates on mats, and Abaye objected.
16.turn: Abaye pointed out that not even a creditor could collect from movable property.
16.outcome: Rav Yosef said he meant ripe dates still attached to the tree; the narrative ends as a legal exchange.
16.summary: Someone came to Rav Yosef about a daughter's sustenance, and he told the sons to give it from dates laid on mats. Abaye objected that even a creditor could not collect that way. Rav Yosef answered that he meant dates still fit for mats, which are attached to the ground.
16.missing: It is a short ruling and challenge exchange rather than a full story.

17.actor: Rabbi Hanina and a poor man he supported
17.event: Rabbi Hanina sent four dinars every Sabbath eve to a poor man, and one day his wife brought it and returned saying the man did not need it.
17.turn: She had overheard people asking him whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
17.outcome: Rabbi Hanina answered with Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should be grateful to swindlers because they excuse us from sin.
17.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a poor man four dinars before the Sabbath. One day his wife delivered it and came back saying the man did not need it, since she had heard people asking him whether he ate off silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina replied that, as Rabbi Elazar said, we should be grateful to swindlers.
17.missing: Segment 4 breaks off mid-sentence and segment 5 completes it.

18.actor: A man who left a silver goblet with Hasa, and Rav Nahman
18.event: A man deposited a silver goblet at Hasa's house, Hasa died without saying anything, and the claimant came before Rav Nahman.
18.turn: Rav Nahman reasoned that Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark, provided he did not frequent the house.
18.outcome: The goblet was awarded to the depositor by implication.
18.summary: A man had deposited a silver goblet in the house of Hasa, who died without leaving instructions. The case went to Rav Nahman, who said Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant had given an identifying sign, so the claim was good unless the claimant was a regular visitor to the house.
18.missing: The final award is implied rather than stated outright.

19.event: Shimon HaAmasoni expounded every occurrence of the word et in the Torah until he reached 'et the Lord your God you shall fear' and withdrew.
19.turn: His students asked what would become of all his earlier expositions.
19.outcome: He said he got reward for both expounding and withdrawing, until Rabbi Akiva later taught that the word includes Torah scholars.
19.summary: Shimon HaAmasoni used to derive new laws from every et in the Torah. When he reached the verse about fearing God he stopped, since nothing could be added to God's fear. His students asked what would become of his earlier teachings and he said he was rewarded equally for expounding and for withdrawing, until Rabbi Akiva later explained that this et includes Torah scholars.

20.actor: Rav Malkiyyu and a deaf-mute neighbor
20.event: Rav Malkiyyu married a deaf-mute man in his neighborhood to a woman, and the deaf-mute wrote her a marriage contract of four hundred zuz from his property.
20.turn: Although a deaf-mute is not obligated to write one, Malkiyyu secured her a contract.
20.outcome: Rava praised Rav Malkiyyu's wisdom, explaining his reasoning that it is like buying a maidservant for him.
20.summary: A deaf-mute man lived near Rav Malkiyyu, who arranged his marriage and had him write his wife a four-hundred-zuz marriage contract. Rava praised Rav Malkiyyu's wisdom, explaining he reasoned that if the man's needs would justify buying a maidservant for him, a wife who also serves him is all the more justified.
